forms.why_en: Speech shortens minä to mä. Books write minä.
Speech drops the l and stretches the vowel: olen becomes oon. Books write olen. From olla, to be.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.

The partitive of mikä, what. Mitä saa olla? means What can I get you?
Tapahtua in the past tense: tapahtui. Speech drops the final i: tapahtu.
Läpäistä changes to läpäis- with -i- for the past and -n for 'I'. Speech drops an i: läpäsin.
Suomi with -n, and i turns to e: suomen kurssi, a Finnish course.
Adds -n for the thing you pass: koe becomes kokeen.
Tietää changes to ties- for something that already happened, then -in for 'I': tiesin.
Speech shortens että to et. Books write että.
Speech shortens sinä to sä. Books write sinä.
Pystyä drops the last ä and takes -t for 'you': pystyt.
The illative singular of se 'it': siihen, 'into it, for it'. People say it the same way.
Olla, to be, in the past tense with -n for 'I': olin.
Books write todella. In speech people use tosi, 'really', instead.
Describes how someone feels, from hermostua, to get nervous. Speech drops the final t: hermostunu.
Speech shortens mutta to mut. Books write mutta.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Voida drops -da and takes -t for 'you': voit.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Speech turns eä into ee: ylpee. Books write ylpeä.

forms.form_name_en: elative singular, with the possessive ending for your
forms.why_en: Itse with -stä and -si for 'your': itsestäsi. Speech drops the last i: itsestäs.
Joo is the everyday spoken yes. Books write kyllä.

forms.form_name_en: present tense, passive, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: Juhlitaan (let's celebrate) with the question ending -ko: juhlitaanko. Speech says juhlitaanks.
Adds -lla for a time of day: ilta becomes illalla, the t turning to l. Speech shortens -lla to -l: illalla becomes illal.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Muu (other) becomes muuta. Ilman muuta means 'of course' or 'definitely'.
